A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, title, core benchmark, and downstream tasks. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison; retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original sampling experiments across 11 models and 15 distributions, sample-size analyses, and downstream MCQ and attribute-generation results, including single-attribute experiments in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds decoding ablations, expanded sample-size experiments, a bivariate Gaussian evaluation, and significance-threshold sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The batch-generation and stateless single-sample procedures remain unchanged. v2 expands their evaluation without introducing a new sampler, architecture, training objective, or inference algorithm. Appendix E identifies its fuller prompt as documentation of the original experiment.

E1.justification: The original 15 distributions and downstream tasks remain. Appendix B adds a correlated bivariate Gaussian with correlation 0.5, evaluating both marginals and Y conditional on X > 0. This adds dependence-sensitive coverage. Bernoulli's inclusion in the expanded sample-size analysis uses an already covered distribution.

E2.justification: Kimi-K2 joins DeepSeek-V3.2 in the existing Gaussian sample-size comparison in Figure 3. The main 11-model comparison and six-model downstream comparison retain their original participants.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands the evaluation design: temperature sweeps over 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, and 1.2; top-p sweeps over 0.9, 0.95, and 1.0; expanded sample-size testing; and marginal and conditional testing for the bivariate experiment. The original default settings, N=1000 benchmark, and dual protocols remain; these additions do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices A and D newly test sensitivity to decoding parameters and significance thresholds. Figures 3–4 extend the earlier DeepSeek Gaussian sample-size analysis to Kimi-K2 and Bernoulli. Appendix B additionally examines whether marginal agreement accompanies conditional fidelity. Together these substantially broaden the robustness and diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix D adds significance-cutoff sensitivity at alpha=0.05 and 0.005 alongside 0.01. Table 6 newly reports five repeated attempts for unparseable GPT-4o batch outputs at temperature 1.2. No general increase in repeated runs, seed reporting, or confidence-interval reporting is documented.

E6.justification: Main Tables 2–5 and the retained single-attribute tables keep their results, but v1 Table 6 is extensively revised as v2 Table 9. For example, GPT-4o's aggregate batch pass rate changes from 33% to 40%, matching the unchanged main Table 2; Gemini-3's batch Tier III W1 changes from 14.02 to 1.05. The reported median changes from 13% to 7%. New decoding, scaling, bivariate, and threshold results add substantial evidence.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(4), the stationary mismatch formulation, and the correction/drift identity are retained. Clarifying N0 as the smallest evaluated horizon and specifying a standard bivariate Gaussian test target add explanation and experimental specification, without substantive new mathematical reasoning or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims remain: unreliable native sampling, protocol asymmetry, worsening fidelity with complexity and sampling horizon, downstream distributional bias, and the need for external sampling tools. The corrected median and additional experiments update evidence without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the claim that temperature 1.0 maximizes entropy and isolates intrinsic bias with a practical rationale for default decoding. New appendices interpret failures as persisting across decoding choices and significance thresholds, and distinguish marginal from conditional fidelity. The main mechanism explanations and Section 7 limitations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data access statement and link, a representative original batch prompt in Appendix E/Table 11, and SciPy in the reference-generation description. Conversely, Section 3.2 removes v1's explicit 50-bin, fixed-effective-support KL specification. These are documentation changes; the linked resources were not externally verified.

R1.justification: Appendix E adds Xu and Ma (2025) on counting difficulties and Yuan et al. (2025) on length constraints to motivate prompt requirements. The main related-work discussion and positioning against earlier sampling studies remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized abstract and explanatory edits, revised decoding and KL descriptions, terminology refinements, and expanded appendix organization. Most main-text prose and section order are retained; the added scientific material does not constitute an extensive narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 3 expands from three panels for one model to six panels for two models, and Figure 4 adds six Bernoulli panels. Five new tables present decoding sweeps, bivariate results, threshold sensitivity, and a sampling prompt. Figure 1 is updated, existing displays are relocated, and numerical-table captions move below their tables.

improvement.justification: The new decoding and threshold checks address robustness gaps in v1, while corrected aggregate summaries resolve inconsistencies with the retained main results. Expanded sampling analyses and prompt/access disclosures also improve checkability. These are clear but bounded gains: Section 6 still claims no Cauchy or chi-square passes despite counterexamples in Table 2, and v2 removes the explicit KL histogram settings.
